notes.front: In Scrum.org's learning material, who counts as a stakeholder?
notes.back: Anyone affected by the product's outcome who has an interest in the product succeeding.
notes.explanation: Scrum.org treats working with these people as central to any product development, because only they can give the feedback that shows whether the product meets their needs.
notes.example: Like the people with a seat at a town-planning meeting about a new park: residents, the council's budget office and the firm that will build it all have a stake in how it turns out.
notes.source: Scrum.org learning series, “Stakeholders and Customers”, “Who are Stakeholders?”
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: In Scrum.org's list of stakeholder kinds, who are the customers?
notes.back: The people who use the product and the people who buy it.
notes.explanation: Scrum.org lists customers as one kind of stakeholder, alongside other kinds that neither use nor buy the product.
notes.example: Like a school's reading app: the pupils who read with it and the head teacher who pays the licence are both customers, though only one of them uses it.
notes.source: Scrum.org learning series, “Stakeholders and Customers”, “Who are Stakeholders?”
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: What does an organization's Mission Statement express, in Scrum.org's Business Strategy material?
notes.back: The organization's purpose: the reason it exists, focused on what it is now.
notes.explanation: It looks at the present, which is what sets it apart from the Vision Statement.
notes.example: Like a bakery saying it is there to sell fresh bread to its street every morning: a statement of today's purpose, not of future plans.
notes.source: Scrum.org learning series, “Business Strategy”
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: What does an organization's Vision Statement express, in Scrum.org's Business Strategy material?
notes.back: The organization's long-term aspirations: what it hopes to achieve in the future.
notes.explanation: It names where the organization wants to get to but leaves out how it will get there.
notes.example: Like a cycling club aiming to have every child in its town able to ride safely one day: a destination, with no route attached.
notes.source: Scrum.org learning series, “Business Strategy”
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: What does a Product Vision describe, in Scrum.org's material?
notes.back: The purpose of a product: the value it should deliver and who receives that value.
notes.explanation: Scrum.org says a vision works when people connect with it both emotionally and practically.
notes.example: Like a sentence on a library's new booking system saying it lets people who work shifts borrow books without queuing: a purpose and an audience, not a feature list.
notes.source: Scrum.org learning series, “Product Vision”, “What is a Product Vision”
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: Where does Business Strategy sit between an organization's mission and vision and its products, in Scrum.org's material?
notes.back: The organization's mission and vision inform it, and it in turn informs the vision of each product.
notes.explanation: Scrum.org places it in the middle of a chain: organization-level statements shape it, and it shapes each product's direction.
notes.example: Like a supermarket chain's plan to move into home delivery: shaped by why the chain exists and where it wants to be, and shaping what its app team aims for.
notes.source: Scrum.org, Professional Scrum Competency “Managing Products with Agility”, business strategy focus area
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: Which two qualities does Scrum.org say a Product Vision should combine so that it inspires creativity in the Scrum Team?
notes.back: It should be both aspirational and actionable.
notes.explanation: With both qualities, Scrum.org says, the vision lets the Scrum Team work creatively together with stakeholders.
notes.source: Scrum.org learning series, “Product Vision”, “What is a Product Vision”
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: Who owns the Product Vision, according to Scrum.org?
notes.back: The Product Owner.
notes.explanation: Ownership does not mean working alone: Scrum.org says developing the vision needs input from stakeholders and the Scrum Team.
notes.source: Scrum.org learning series, “Product Vision”, “What is a Product Vision”
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: Scrum.org says a good Product Vision is built {{c1::incrementally}}, so there are repeated chances to inspect and adapt it.
notes.back: incrementally
notes.explanation: Building it in steps is what creates the repeated chances to inspect and adapt it.
notes.source: Scrum.org learning series, “Product Vision”, “What is a Product Vision”
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: A new Product Owner spends a month writing the final Product Vision alone, then hands it to the Scrum Team and stakeholders as finished. What does Scrum.org's guidance suggest?
notes.back: Keep ownership, but build the vision in steps with input from stakeholders and the Scrum Team.
notes.choices:
A) Fine: the Product Owner owns the vision, so nobody else takes part
B) Keep ownership, but build the vision in steps with input from stakeholders and the Scrum Team
C) Hand the vision to the stakeholders, who should own it
notes.choicesExplained: A: ownership is the Product Owner's, but Scrum.org says others' input is needed. C: Scrum.org names the Product Owner as the owner, not the stakeholders.
notes.explanation: Scrum.org pairs ownership by the Product Owner with input from others and with incremental building.
notes.source: Scrum.org learning series, “Product Vision”, “What is a Product Vision”
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: A draft Product Vision for a parking app reads: “dark mode, map view, receipts by email”. What is it missing, going by Scrum.org's description?
notes.back: The value the product should deliver and to whom it delivers that value.
notes.choices:
A) A release date for each feature
B) The value the product should deliver and to whom it delivers that value
C) A list of the Developers who will build it
notes.choicesExplained: A: Scrum.org describes a vision by purpose and value, not by dates. C: who builds the product is not part of Scrum.org's description of a vision.
notes.explanation: Scrum.org describes a vision as stating purpose, value and recipient; a list of features states none of these.
notes.source: Scrum.org learning series, “Product Vision”, “What is a Product Vision”
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: What two elements does Scrum.org say form the context in which a Product Vision exists?
notes.back: Business Strategy and Product Strategy.
notes.explanation: Scrum.org says the vision should stand on its own as a clear statement of intent, yet still sits within these two.
notes.source: Scrum.org learning series, “Product Vision”, “What is a Product Vision”
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: Which Product Vision technique on Scrum.org has a team write about an imagined future, and is also called Newspaper Headline or Cover Story?
notes.back: The Future Press Release.
notes.explanation: Scrum.org presents it as a way to encourage visionary thinking and agreement on the outcomes wanted from the product.
notes.source: Scrum.org learning series, “Product Vision”, linked resource on the Future Press Release
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: Which widely used Product Vision template on Scrum.org produces a short fill-in sentence that boils the vision down to its essence?
notes.back: The Elevator Pitch.
notes.explanation: Scrum.org ties it to the elevator test: saying the idea in the time a short lift ride allows.
notes.source: Scrum.org learning series, “Product Vision”, linked resource on the Elevator Pitch
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: Which Product Vision technique on Scrum.org is offered as a way to keep a vision customer-focused rather than a list of features?
notes.back: The Product Box.
notes.explanation: Scrum.org says some teams fall into describing features when writing a vision, although the product exists to deliver value to customers.
notes.source: Scrum.org learning series, “Product Vision”, linked resource on the Product Box
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: What does Scrum.org say a Vision Statement leaves out?
notes.back: How the organization will achieve the vision.
notes.explanation: It describes the hoped-for future only; the means belong elsewhere, such as in Business Strategy.
notes.source: Scrum.org learning series, “Business Strategy”
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: How does a Mission Statement differ from a Vision Statement in time, according to Scrum.org?
notes.back: The Mission Statement is about what the organization is today; the Vision Statement is about what it hopes to achieve long term.
notes.explanation: One gives the present reason for existing, the other a future aspiration.
notes.source: Scrum.org learning series, “Business Strategy”
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: A charity writes: “We run food banks that give free groceries to families in our county who cannot afford food.” Which statement is this, in Scrum.org's terms?
notes.back: A Mission Statement.
notes.choices:
A) A Mission Statement
B) A Vision Statement
C) A Product Vision
notes.choicesExplained: B: a Vision Statement looks to long-term aspirations; this says why the charity exists now. C: a Product Vision is about one product, not the whole organization.
notes.explanation: It gives the organization's present purpose, which is what a Mission Statement expresses.
notes.source: Scrum.org learning series, “Business Strategy”
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: A rail operator writes: “By 2040 we hope to be the first choice for every journey under 500 kilometres.” Which statement is this, in Scrum.org's terms?
notes.back: A Vision Statement.
notes.choices:
A) A Mission Statement
B) A Vision Statement
C) A Sprint Goal
notes.choicesExplained: A: a Mission Statement says why the organization exists today, not what it hopes to reach. C: a Sprint Goal is the single objective for one Sprint, not an organization's long-term aim.
notes.explanation: It is a long-term aspiration and says nothing of how it will be reached, which matches a Vision Statement.
notes.source: Scrum.org learning series, “Business Strategy”
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: Who does Scrum.org say is typically accountable for creating an organization's mission and vision?
notes.back: Senior executives.
notes.explanation: Scrum.org adds that the mission and vision drive the organization's business strategy.
notes.source: Scrum.org learning series, “Business Strategy”
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: What does Scrum.org say an organization uses to inspect and adapt its Business Strategy?
notes.back: Feedback gathered from delivering product Increments.
notes.explanation: What is learned from delivering Increments feeds back into the strategy, which in turn informs each Product Vision.
notes.source: Scrum.org, Professional Scrum Competency “Managing Products with Agility”, business strategy focus area
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: A firm fixed a five-year plan to win large corporate clients. Three released Increments show that almost all paying users are sole traders. What fits Scrum.org's view of Business Strategy?
notes.back: Inspect the strategy against this feedback and adapt it, which may change the product's vision.
notes.choices:
A) Keep the plan: strategy is set once by senior executives
B) Inspect the strategy against this feedback and adapt it, which may change the product's vision
C) Leave strategy alone and let the Developers change the Sprint Goal only
notes.choicesExplained: A: Scrum.org says strategy is inspected and adapted from Increment feedback. C: the feedback bears on strategy itself, and strategy informs the product's vision.
notes.explanation: Scrum.org describes strategy as adapted from Increment feedback and as informing each Product Vision.
notes.source: Scrum.org, Professional Scrum Competency “Managing Products with Agility”, business strategy focus area
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: Which kind of stakeholder in Scrum.org's list covers company management and functions such as human resources, compliance and finance?
notes.back: Internal stakeholders.
notes.explanation: They sit inside the organization but are affected by, and interested in, how the product turns out.
notes.source: Scrum.org learning series, “Stakeholders and Customers”, “Who are Stakeholders?”
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: Which kind of stakeholder in Scrum.org's list covers suppliers, vendors and other business partners?
notes.back: Partners.
notes.explanation: They are outside the organization but take part in the business around the product.
notes.source: Scrum.org learning series, “Stakeholders and Customers”, “Who are Stakeholders?”
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: Which kind of stakeholder in Scrum.org's list covers outside voices such as trade bodies, the media and industry analysts?
notes.back: Influencers.
notes.explanation: They neither use nor supply the product, yet Scrum.org still counts them as stakeholders.
notes.source: Scrum.org learning series, “Stakeholders and Customers”, “Who are Stakeholders?”
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: A hospital builds a patient-booking app. The firm that hosts its servers is worried about a planned change. In Scrum.org's list, what kind of stakeholder is the hosting firm?
notes.back: A partner.
notes.choices:
A) A customer
B) An internal stakeholder
C) A partner
notes.choicesExplained: A: customers use or buy the product; the host does neither. B: internal stakeholders are the hospital's own management and departments.
notes.explanation: A supplier to the product falls under partners in Scrum.org's list.
notes.source: Scrum.org learning series, “Stakeholders and Customers”, “Who are Stakeholders?”
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: A council buys a parking app licence for its car parks, and drivers pay for parking through it. In Scrum.org's terms, which of them are customers?
notes.back: Both: the council buys the product and the drivers use it.
notes.choices:
A) Only the council, because it pays for the licence
B) Only the drivers, because they use the app
C) Both: the council buys the product and the drivers use it
notes.choicesExplained: A: users count as customers too. B: buyers count as customers too.
notes.explanation: Scrum.org defines customers as both the users and the buyers of the product.
notes.source: Scrum.org learning series, “Stakeholders and Customers”, “Who are Stakeholders?”
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: Why does Scrum.org call engaging stakeholders central to product development?
notes.back: Only the stakeholders themselves can tell the team whether the product meets their needs and expectations.
notes.explanation: The feedback has to come from the people affected; the Scrum Team cannot supply it for them.
notes.source: Scrum.org learning series, “Stakeholders and Customers”, “Who are Stakeholders?”
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: In Scrum.org's material, how do customers relate to stakeholders?
notes.back: Customers are one kind of stakeholder; stakeholders also include internal people, partners and influencers.
notes.explanation: Every customer is a stakeholder, but many stakeholders never use or buy the product.
notes.source: Scrum.org learning series, “Stakeholders and Customers”, “Who are Stakeholders?”
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: In the Scrum Guide, who is responsible for all product-related activities, stakeholder collaboration included?
notes.back: The Scrum Team.
notes.explanation: The Guide lists stakeholder collaboration first among the product activities the whole Scrum Team is responsible for.
notes.evidence: The Scrum Team is responsible for all product-related activities from stakeholder collaboration, verification, maintenance, operation, experimentation, research and development, and anything else that might be required.
notes.source: The Scrum Guide (November 2020), “Scrum Team”
notes.sourceLicence: B · CC BY-SA 4.0

notes.front: At Sprint Planning the whole Scrum Team defines a Sprint Goal that communicates {{c1::why the Sprint is valuable to stakeholders}}.
notes.back: why the Sprint is valuable to stakeholders
notes.explanation: The Product Owner first proposes how the product could gain value and utility in the Sprint; the whole team then turns that into the goal.
notes.evidence: The Product Owner proposes how the product could increase its value and utility in the current Sprint. The whole Scrum Team then collaborates to define a Sprint Goal that communicates why the Sprint is valuable to stakeholders.
notes.source: The Scrum Guide (November 2020), “Sprint Planning”, Topic One
notes.sourceLicence: B · CC BY-SA 4.0

notes.front: At the end of Sprint Planning the Sprint Goal reads “Finish tickets 412 to 419”. The sales director says she cannot tell why this Sprint matters to her. What does the Scrum Guide suggest is wrong?
notes.back: The Sprint Goal should communicate why the Sprint is valuable to stakeholders; a list of tickets does not.
notes.choices:
A) Nothing: the Sprint Goal is only for the Developers
B) The Sprint Goal should communicate why the Sprint is valuable to stakeholders; a list of tickets does not
C) The sales director should have been given the Sprint Backlog to approve
notes.choicesExplained: A: the Guide says the goal communicates the Sprint's value to stakeholders. C: the Guide gives stakeholders no approval step over the Sprint Backlog.
notes.explanation: The Guide defines the Sprint Goal by what it tells stakeholders about the Sprint's value.
notes.evidence: The whole Scrum Team then collaborates to define a Sprint Goal that communicates why the Sprint is valuable to stakeholders.
notes.source: The Scrum Guide (November 2020), “Sprint Planning”, Topic One
notes.sourceLicence: B · CC BY-SA 4.0

notes.front: What is the purpose of the Sprint Review?
notes.back: To inspect the outcome of the Sprint and determine future adaptations.
notes.explanation: The Scrum Team shows its results to key stakeholders and they discuss progress toward the Product Goal.
notes.evidence: The purpose of the Sprint Review is to inspect the outcome of the Sprint and determine future adaptations. The Scrum Team presents the results of their work to key stakeholders and progress toward the Product Goal is discussed.
notes.source: The Scrum Guide (November 2020), “Sprint Review”
notes.sourceLicence: B · CC BY-SA 4.0

notes.front: At the Sprint Review, what do the Scrum Team and stakeholders review before deciding together what to do next?
notes.back: What was accomplished in the Sprint and what has changed in their environment.
notes.explanation: The Guide adds that the Product Backlog may also be adjusted to meet new opportunities.
notes.evidence: During the event, the Scrum Team and stakeholders review what was accomplished in the Sprint and what has changed in their environment. Based on this information, attendees collaborate on what to do next. The Product Backlog may also be adjusted to meet new opportunities.
notes.source: The Scrum Guide (November 2020), “Sprint Review”
notes.sourceLicence: B · CC BY-SA 4.0

notes.front: The Scrum Guide calls the Sprint Review a {{c1::working session}}, which the Scrum Team should avoid limiting to a presentation.
notes.back: working session
notes.explanation: The same passage says attendees collaborate on what to do next and may adjust the Product Backlog.
notes.evidence: Based on this information, attendees collaborate on what to do next. The Product Backlog may also be adjusted to meet new opportunities. The Sprint Review is a working session and the Scrum Team should avoid limiting it to a presentation.
notes.source: The Scrum Guide (November 2020), “Sprint Review”
notes.sourceLicence: B · CC BY-SA 4.0

notes.front: A Product Owner runs every Sprint Review as a 40-slide talk, then ends the meeting with no time for questions. Which change best fits the Scrum Guide?
notes.back: Make it a working session where the Scrum Team and stakeholders collaborate on what to do next.
notes.choices:
A) Add more slides so stakeholders see every detail
B) Make it a working session where the Scrum Team and stakeholders collaborate on what to do next
C) Send the slides by email and cancel the Sprint Review
notes.choicesExplained: A: more slides is still only a presentation. C: the Sprint Review is a Scrum event where the outcome is inspected with stakeholders, which an email does not do.
notes.explanation: The Guide asks the Scrum Team not to limit the Sprint Review to a presentation.
notes.evidence: The Sprint Review is a working session and the Scrum Team should avoid limiting it to a presentation.
notes.source: The Scrum Guide (November 2020), “Sprint Review”
notes.sourceLicence: B · CC BY-SA 4.0

notes.front: The Sprint Review is timeboxed to a maximum of {{c1::four hours}} for a one-month Sprint.
notes.back: four hours
notes.explanation: For shorter Sprints the Guide says the event is usually shorter.
notes.evidence: The Sprint Review is the second to last event of the Sprint and is timeboxed to a maximum of four hours for a one-month Sprint. For shorter Sprints, the event is usually shorter.
notes.source: The Scrum Guide (November 2020), “Sprint Review”
notes.sourceLicence: B · CC BY-SA 4.0

notes.front: A team with two-week Sprints books six hours for its Sprint Review. What does the Scrum Guide say?
notes.back: Too long: the maximum is four hours even for a one-month Sprint, and shorter Sprints usually have shorter reviews.
notes.choices:
A) Fine: the timebox is eight hours
B) Too long: the maximum is four hours even for a one-month Sprint, and shorter Sprints usually have shorter reviews
C) Fine, as long as the stakeholders agree
notes.choicesExplained: A: eight hours is the Sprint Planning maximum, not the Sprint Review's. C: stakeholder agreement does not change the timebox.
notes.explanation: Six hours exceeds the four-hour maximum that applies to the longest possible Sprint.
notes.evidence: timeboxed to a maximum of four hours for a one-month Sprint. For shorter Sprints, the event is usually shorter.
notes.source: The Scrum Guide (November 2020), “Sprint Review”
notes.sourceLicence: B · CC BY-SA 4.0

notes.front: Among the ways the Scrum Master serves the organization, what does the Scrum Guide say about stakeholders?
notes.back: The Scrum Master removes barriers between stakeholders and Scrum Teams.
notes.explanation: It sits in the Guide's list of ways the Scrum Master serves the organization, not only the Scrum Team.
notes.evidence: Removing barriers between stakeholders and Scrum Teams.
notes.source: The Scrum Guide (November 2020), “Scrum Master”
notes.sourceLicence: B · CC BY-SA 4.0
